name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 10 February 1973

clue.text: Flashy sort of vessel?'/

blocks.note: surface reading: showy, ostentatious, as if describing a gaudy boat
setter's reading: a ship whose whole job is to flash a warning beam at sea

explanation.surface: A gaudy, showy boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flashy' means showy on the surface, but here it is literal: the vessel gives out flashes. The trailing marks after the question mark are scan noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A moored ship carrying a beacon to warn mariners off shoals is literally a vessel that flashes.

clue.text: Female worker was relieved

definitions.note: the answer is a place name; the definition describes what famously happened to it

blocks.note: a lady is a woman
a smith is a metalworker

explanation.surface: A working woman finally got a break.
explanation.walkthrough: Ladysmith is a town in South Africa besieged by the Boers in 1899 and famously relieved in 1900, so 'was relieved' is a cryptic pointer to a town, not a feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: The Relief of Ladysmith ended a four-month siege in the Boer War, so this town is the one that was relieved.

clue.text: A gift from Ulysses?

blocks.note: first meaning: a sum of money given, as for study
second meaning: Ulysses S. ..., US Civil War general and president

explanation.surface: A present from the Greek hero Ulysses, like the wooden horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulysses suggests the Greek hero and his Trojan Horse, but the Ulysses meant is an American general.
explanation.definitionFit: A grant is money given for a purpose, and Grant was the surname of Ulysses S., the Union general.

clue.text: Wrong river to find this creature

blocks.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law
the Oise is a river in northern France

explanation.surface: Taking the wrong river to track down some animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' looks like an instruction to rearrange river, but it is the legal noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The tortoise is a slow land reptile with a domed shell, a particular animal or creature.

clue.text: Pianist brings nothing into German port

indicators.note: into says one thing is put inside another, so the zero goes within the port's name

blocks.note: Hamburg is Germany's largest port
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A concert pianist arrives in a German harbour city empty-handed.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Hambourg was a Russian-born British concert pianist, famous in the early twentieth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Hambourg was a celebrated virtuoso who played piano recitals worldwide, so he is a pianist.

clue.text: Pictures found in separating some litter

indicators.note: to separate a thing is to come between its parts, so the outer word is split around the other

blocks.note: a litter is a set of young animals born together, such as pups
taken as written

explanation.surface: Photographs discovered while sorting out rubbish or a brood of animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Pin-ups are pictures of glamorous people pinned to a wall, a particular kind of picture.

clue.text: Strokes made in set by way of return

indicators.note: a return is a trip back, so the word for way is written back to front

blocks.note: to set something down is to put it
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Shots played during a tennis set by way of returning serve.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis words set and return push toward rallies, but the strokes are golf ones on the green.
explanation.definitionFit: On a golf green each gentle stroke toward the hole is a putt, so strokes there are putts.

clue.text: Mountain rises in south ern steppes

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means reading upward, so the word for mountain is written backwards

blocks.note: an alp is a high mountain
taken as written
the scan splits southern; S is the abbreviation for south or southern

explanation.surface: A peak towers above the steppes of the south.
explanation.definitionFit: Steppes are the vast flat grasslands of Russia and Central Asia, which are plains.

clue.text: Easily managed vehicle is back on list

indicators.note: going back means running the other way, so the word for vehicle is spelt in reverse

blocks.note: a cart is a simple wheeled vehicle
a table is a list of figures or items

explanation.surface: A car that handles nicely is back on the sales list.
explanation.definitionFit: A tractable person or thing is docile and controllable, so tractable is a synonym for easy to handle.

clue.text: Lover was awkward at home

indicators.note: something awkward is clumsy and out of order, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
to be at home is to be in

explanation.surface: A boyfriend felt clumsy staying in.
explanation.definitionFit: Swain is a poetic, old-fashioned word for a young man courting a woman, her suitor.

clue.text: Indian city shown in obscure plan

indicators.note: a thing shown in something else sits inside it, so the city goes within the word for obscure

blocks.note: dim means faint or obscure
Agra is the Indian city of the Taj Mahal

explanation.surface: An Indian city appears on a hard-to-read map.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawn plan of a building or machine is a diagram, a synonym in the technical sense.

clue.text: Falls for a redhead once more in retirement

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the whole string is read from its end

blocks.note: taken as written
the head of red is its first letter
once more means again

explanation.surface: Someone retiring falls in love with a red-haired woman all over again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls for' reads as falling in love, but Falls is the definition and 'for' only joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Niagara is the famous waterfall on the US-Canada border, so it names a particular set of falls.

clue.text: The fight in Barset town hall?

indicators.note: in says the answer lies inside the run of words that follows, spanning a word break

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of Barset and the start of town

explanation.surface: A row breaks out in the town hall of Barset, Trollope's imaginary cathedral county.
explanation.walkthrough: Barset is Anthony Trollope's fictional county, home of his clerical novels, which makes a council-chamber squabble feel like literature.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is an informal word for a brief, heated quarrel or scuffle between people.

clue.text: Kent town provides replacement for GP in Troon

indicators.note: a replacement puts things in new positions, so the letters are set out afresh

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written: Troon is a Scottish golfing town

explanation.surface: A town in Kent sends a locum to stand in for the family doctor in Troon.
explanation.walkthrough: A GP is a family doctor, and 'replacement' looks like a locum, but it signals rearranging letters. Orpington is a town in Kent, on the southeast edge of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Orpington lies in the historic county of Kent, so it is a Kent town.

clue.text: Eastern religious types 'ave a go, with diligence

indicators.note: the apostrophe drops the opening aitch Cockney-style, telling us to drop that letter from the first word too

blocks.note: Hindus follow India's main religion
to have a go is to have a try

explanation.surface: Cockney encouragement to some Eastern worshippers to have a go and work hard.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped aitch in 'ave is the signal: the religious types lose their opening H the same Cockney way.
explanation.definitionFit: Industry in its older sense is steady hard work, a synonym of diligence.

clue.text: A hundred tales of French romance, possibly

indicators.note: possibly hints that the word is only one arrangement of its letters, and another is wanted

blocks.note: de is French for of
taken as written

explanation.surface: A collection of a hundred French love stories, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French romance' looks like a genre, but French only translates of.
explanation.definitionFit: Boccaccio's fourteenth-century Italian collection holds one hundred stories told over ten days.

clue.text: Come up against an objection

blocks.note: an and a are the same article
a but is an objection, as in no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: Running into an objection to a plan.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things that abut meet edge to edge, pressing up against one another, as neighbouring plots do.

clue.text: A conveyance, or an accolade?

blocks.note: first meaning: the legal document proving ownership of property
second meaning, playful: the dubbing that creates a knight is an act, or deed, that bestows a title

explanation.surface: Asking whether something is a means of transport or a tribute.
explanation.walkthrough: A conveyance sounds like a vehicle, but in law it is the document transferring land. The second sense is a pun, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The paper recording ownership of land is the legal conveyance, and knighting is an act that confers a title.

clue.text: Control of course needed for such passengers

definitions.note: used attributively, as in steerage passengers

blocks.note: first meaning: the act of steering a ship
second meaning: the cheapest class of berth on an old liner, near the rudder

explanation.surface: Passengers need someone to keep the ship on course.
explanation.definitionFit: Steering a vessel is its steerage, and the cheap below-decks class of travel took the same name.

clue.text: Oust from the under world, perhaps

blocks.note: Dis is the Roman god of the dead and his underworld realm
the underworld is perhaps a place: the setter reads it as Dis place

explanation.surface: Driving someone out of the criminal underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is loose: the underworld, perhaps, is Dis's place, so the two halves read as Dis place.
explanation.definitionFit: To displace someone is to push them out of their position, which is what oust means.

clue.text: Cut work of poor writer?

blocks.note: first meaning: to chop roughly
second meaning: ... work, routine writing churned out for pay

explanation.surface: An editor slashes the copy of a bad author.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both rough chopping and the dull writing of a jobbing scribbler, so each half fits.

clue.text: Direction to aircraft appears harsh

blocks.note: S for south, a compass direction
the Trident was a British airliner of the 1960s and 70s

explanation.surface: An air-traffic controller's instruction to a plane sounds brusque.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direction to aircraft' reads as a radio order; it is a compass point placed next to a named airliner.
explanation.definitionFit: A strident voice is loud and grating, so the word works as a synonym for harsh in sound.

clue.text: Sayings in yearly letters to The Times?

blocks.note: AD, anno Domini, are the letters placed before a year
ages are times or eras

explanation.surface: Old sayings quoted in annual letters to The Times newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times is the London newspaper, famous for readers' letters, but here it just means eras.
explanation.definitionFit: Adages are old proverbs, short traditional sayings that express a general truth.

clue.text: Compose a feature film?

blocks.note: first meaning: to invent or put together
second meaning: cosmetics, a thin film laid on the facial features

explanation.surface: Writing the script for a full-length movie.
explanation.walkthrough: A feature film is a cinema movie on the surface; the setter means a film, a coating, on the features of the face.
explanation.definitionFit: To make up a story is to compose it, and makeup is cosmetic coating on the features.

clue.text: Means to be in time to change without delay

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters of time are rearranged
to be in something is to sit inside it, so the word for means goes within the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written
media is the plural of medium, a means of doing something

explanation.surface: A way to be punctual and alter plans straight away.
explanation.definitionFit: Something immediate happens at once, with no interval, which is what without delay describes.

clue.text: Drive for a mile, roughly, round Polish capital

indicators.note: a capital is the letter at the start of a word, so only the first of Polish counts
done roughly, the letters lose their tidy order and come out jumbled
round says the jumbled letters go around the other piece, enclosing it

blocks.note: taken as written
first letter of Polish

explanation.surface: A motorist drives about a mile around Warsaw, the Polish capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish capital' points at Warsaw, but it means the capital letter of the word Polish.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to push or urge forward, the same as to drive someone on.

clue.text: Race course supporter?

blocks.note: first meaning: a horse race with a trophy as prize
second meaning: the dish that holds a course of a meal

explanation.surface: Someone who backs a racecourse, or a fan at the track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race course' reads as one word for a track; split it, and course is a stage of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plate is both a horse race run for a cup and the flat dish a meal's course sits on.

clue.text: A high room for us jolly sailor-boys

definitions.text: A high room for us jolly sailor-boys

blocks.note: taken as written
a loft is a room up under the roof

explanation.surface: A line from a sea shanty: up in the rigging is where we jolly sailors go.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: sailors climb up into the rigging, the high place on board.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloft is the nautical word for up in the masts and rigging, where sailors work high above deck.

clue.text: Sanctimonious rascal in canoe

blocks.note: pi is slang for pious or sanctimonious
a rogue is a rascal

explanation.surface: A smug villain paddles a canoe.
explanation.walkthrough: PI as a short form of pious is old schoolboy slang the solver may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirogue is a dugout boat of the Caribbean and Louisiana bayous, a kind of canoe.

clue.text: Sea-food for Jack only?

blocks.note: a jack, or jack tar, is a sailor; AB is an able seaman
alone means only, as in he alone knew

explanation.surface: A dish of seafood meant for one man called Jack.
explanation.definitionFit: Abalone is a large edible sea snail prized as a delicacy, hence a kind of seafood.

clue.text: Wrinkles the bride gets after marriage

blocks.note: first meaning: creases in the skin of the face
second meaning: marriage ..., the British name for a wedding certificate

explanation.surface: A joke that married life brings a new wife creases on her face.
explanation.walkthrough: Marriage lines is an old British phrase for the certificate a couple receives at the wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Facial creases are called lines, and the certificate of a wedding is the couple's marriage lines.

clue.text: Quietly took umbrage,1 being introduced

blocks.note: p for piano, the musical mark for soft
to take umbrage at something is to resent it

explanation.surface: Someone silently sulked on being introduced to a stranger.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray 1 after the comma is scan noise and plays no part.
explanation.definitionFit: To present a person to someone is to make a formal introduction, so presented is a synonym.
